title: Jira vs Plane
comparison_markdown:
# Jira vs Plane (2026)

## Overview
Jira and Plane are two project management tools designed to help teams organize and track their work. This comparison is useful for teams currently using Jira who are considering switching to Plane, possibly due to cost or data ownership concerns. The core use case for both tools is issue tracking and project management, and someone would switch if they need more control over their data or a more cost-effective solution.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Jira is a paid tool with a per-user monthly fee, while Plane is free and self-hosted.
* Data ownership: Plane allows teams to host their own data, giving them full control and ownership, while Jira stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Plane requires more technical expertise to set up and configure, while Jira is generally easier to get started with.
* Scalability: Jira is designed to handle large, complex projects and teams, while Plane is better suited for smaller to medium-sized teams.
* Integration with GitHub: Jira has a more comprehensive integration with GitHub, allowing for more seamless issue tracking and project management, while Plane's integration is more limited.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Jira | Plane |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.75-$14.50/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $387.50-$725/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,550-$2,900/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Jira:**
* Comprehensive project management features
* Robust integration with other Atlassian tools
* Scalable and reliable
* Good customer support
* Limited control over data ownership
**Plane:**
* Free and self-hosted
* Full control over data ownership
* Highly customizable
* Open-source and community-driven
* Limited integration with other tools

## When to Choose Each
Jira is a good choice for large, complex teams that need a robust and scalable project management solution. It's also a good fit for teams that are already invested in the Atlassian ecosystem and want to take advantage of its integrations with other tools. On the other hand, Plane is a good choice for smaller to medium-sized teams that want a free and self-hosted solution with full control over their data. It's also a good fit for teams that value customization and community-driven development.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Jira data in XML or CSV format.
2. Use the Plane import tool to import your data into Plane.
3. Configure your Plane instance to match your Jira workflow.
4. Update any integrations or customizations to work with Plane.
5. Test your Plane instance to ensure everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
Plane is not yet production-ready for most users, as it still lacks some of the features and polish of Jira. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Plane's integration with GitHub is limited, which may be a deal-breaker for teams that rely heavily on GitHub. However, for teams that value data ownership and customization, Plane is a good choice, and we recommend switching from Jira to Plane if you have a small to medium-sized team and don't need all the features of Jira.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that don't need robust project management features
* Teams that value data ownership and control
* Teams that are already self-hosting other tools and want to add Plane to their stack
* Teams that are looking for a free and open-source solution
* Teams that don't need integration with GitHub or other tools

## FAQ
### Is Plane free?
Yes, Plane is free and self-hosted.
### Can I migrate my Jira data to Plane?
Yes, you can export your Jira data in XML or CSV format and import it into Plane.
### Does Plane have good customer support?
Plane has a community-driven support model, but it may not be as comprehensive as Jira's support.
### Can I use Plane for large, complex projects?
While Plane can handle smaller to medium-sized projects, it may not be the best fit for large, complex projects that require robust project management features.
### Is Plane available as a cloud-hosted solution?
No, Plane is only available as a self-hosted solution.

# Trello vs WeKan (2026)

## Overview
Trello and WeKan are project management tools that help teams organize and track their work. This comparison is useful for teams considering switching from Trello to WeKan, particularly those who value data ownership and self-hosting. The core use case for both tools is task and project management, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Trello offers a free plan with limited features, while WeKan is free and self-hosted.
* Data ownership: WeKan allows teams to host their data on their own servers, while Trello stores data on its proprietary servers.
* Setup complexity: WeKan requires more technical expertise to set up and maintain, while Trello is easy to use out of the box.
* Scalability: Trello is designed to scale with large teams, while WeKan's scalability depends on the team's server infrastructure.
* Integration: Trello has a wider range of integrations with third-party tools, while WeKan has limited integrations but allows for custom development.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Trello | WeKan |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $5+/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $250/month (Standard plan) | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1000/month (Premium plan) | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Trello
* Easy to use and set up
* Wide range of integrations with third-party tools
* Scalable with large teams
* Mobile apps available
* Limited control over data ownership
### WeKan
* Free and self-hosted
* High degree of customization possible
* Data ownership and control
* Open-source community
* Limited integrations with third-party tools
* Requires technical expertise to set up and maintain

## When to Choose Each
Trello is a good choice for teams who value ease of use and a wide range of integrations with third-party tools. It's suitable for teams of all sizes, from small startups to large enterprises. WeKan, on the other hand, is a good choice for teams who value data ownership and control, and are willing to invest time and resources into setting up and maintaining their own server infrastructure. It's suitable for small to medium-sized teams who are technically savvy.

## Migration Path
1. Export Trello boards as JSON files using the Trello API or a third-party tool.
2. Set up a WeKan server and configure it to import the JSON files.
3. Use the WeKan import tool to migrate the data from Trello to WeKan.
4. Configure any custom workflows or integrations in WeKan.
5. Test the migration to ensure all data has been transferred correctly.

## Our Take
WeKan is not yet production-ready for most users, as it requires a high degree of technical expertise to set up and maintain. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that WeKan's scalability depends on the team's server infrastructure, which can be a bottleneck for large teams. However, for teams who value data ownership and control, WeKan is a good choice, and we recommend switching from Trello to WeKan if you have a small to medium-sized team and are willing to invest time and resources into setting up and maintaining your own server infrastructure.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) who value data ownership and control
* Teams who do not need a wide range of integrations with third-party tools
* Teams who are technically savvy and willing to invest time and resources into setting up and maintaining their own server infrastructure
* Teams who are currently using Trello's free plan and want to avoid paying for upgrades
* Teams who are looking for a self-hosted solution and are willing to customize and develop their own workflows

## FAQ

Yes, you can migrate your Trello boards to WeKan using the Trello API or a third-party tool.
### Is WeKan free?
Yes, WeKan is free and self-hosted.
### Does WeKan have mobile apps?
No, WeKan does not have mobile apps, but it can be accessed through a web browser on mobile devices.
### Can I customize WeKan to fit my team's workflows?
Yes, WeKan allows for a high degree of customization, but it requires technical expertise.

WeKan's scalability depends on the team's server infrastructure, which can be a bottleneck for large teams.

title: Dropbox vs Nextcloud
comparison_markdown:
# Dropbox vs Nextcloud

## Overview

Dropbox is one of the original cloud storage services offering simple file sync. Nextcloud is the most popular self-hosted cloud platform combining file storage, calendar, contacts, video calls, and 400+ apps.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Dropbox charges $9.99-$16.58/user/month; Nextcloud is free to self-host
- **Storage**: Nextcloud storage is limited only by your server disk space
- **Feature breadth**: Nextcloud is far more than storage; it is a full Google Workspace alternative
- **Privacy**: Nextcloud on your own server means only you can access your data
- **Setup**: Dropbox is instant; Nextcloud requires Docker setup

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Dropbox | Nextcloud |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | $9.99-$16.58/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | AGPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | ~$500/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | ~$1,998/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Dropbox

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Nextcloud

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [nextcloud/server](https://github.com/nextcloud/server) * ~27k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Dropbox if:** Dropbox suits individuals or small teams wanting simple reliable file sync with no infrastructure to manage.

**Choose Nextcloud if:** Nextcloud suits privacy-focused organizations wanting to eliminate cloud subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Download all Dropbox files locally, then upload to Nextcloud via the web interface or desktop sync client.

## Our Take

Nextcloud is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Dropbox tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your Nextcloud instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Dropbox, switching to self-hosted Nextcloud will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Dropbox until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Dropbox paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is Nextcloud free to use?
Yes. Nextcloud is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Dropbox to Nextcloud?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Dropbox data, follow the Nextcloud import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Nextcloud get regular updates?
Yes. Nextcloud has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use Nextcloud without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if Nextcloud development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced July 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Dropbox](https://dropbox.com) and [Nextcloud](https://nextcloud.com) before making decisions.*
meta_description: Nextcloud is a free, self-hosted alternative to Dropbox. Compare pricing, features, and migration steps. See full comparison.

# Airtable vs NocoDB (2026)

## Overview
Airtable and NocoDB are two database management tools that help teams organize and manage their data. This comparison is beneficial for teams looking to switch from Airtable to NocoDB, particularly those who value data ownership and a self-hosted solution. The core use case for both tools is to provide a flexible and scalable database solution, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Airtable offers a free plan and paid plans starting at $10-$20 per user per month, while NocoDB is free and self-hosted.
* Data ownership: NocoDB allows teams to have full ownership of their data, while Airtable stores data on its proprietary servers.
* Setup complexity: Airtable has a more user-friendly interface and is generally easier to set up, while NocoDB requires more technical expertise.
* Scalability: Both tools are scalable, but NocoDB's self-hosted nature allows for more flexibility in terms of customization and scalability.
* Feature difference: Airtable has a more comprehensive set of built-in features, including a calendar view and a Kanban board, while NocoDB has a more limited set of features but allows for more customization through its API.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Airtable | NocoDB |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $10-$20/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | AGPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $500-$1000 per month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $2000-$4000 per month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Airtable:**
* Pros:
	+ User-friendly interface
	+ Comprehensive set of built-in features
	+ Scalable and reliable
	+ Integrates with a wide range of third-party apps
	+ Good customer support
* Cons:
	+ Limited control over data ownership
	+ Can be expensive for large teams
	+ Limited customization options
**NocoDB:**
* Pros:
	+ Self-hosted and open-source
	+ Full control over data ownership
	+ Highly customizable
	+ Scalable and flexible
	+ Free
* Cons:
	+ Requires technical expertise to set up and manage
	+ Limited set of built-in features
	+ May require additional development to integrate with third-party apps
	+ Limited customer support

## When to Choose Each
Airtable is a good choice for teams who value ease of use and a comprehensive set of built-in features, and are willing to pay for a proprietary solution. It's particularly well-suited for small to medium-sized teams who need a scalable and reliable database solution. NocoDB, on the other hand, is a good choice for teams who value data ownership and customization, and have the technical expertise to set up and manage a self-hosted solution. It's particularly well-suited for large teams or enterprises who need a highly scalable and flexible database solution.

## Migration Path
1. Export your data from Airtable in CSV or JSON format.
2. Set up a new NocoDB instance on your own server or cloud platform.
3. Use the NocoDB import tool to import your data from the CSV or JSON file.
4. Configure your NocoDB instance to match your Airtable setup, including setting up tables, views, and relationships.
5. Test your NocoDB instance to ensure that everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
NocoDB is not yet production-ready for most users, as it requires technical expertise to set up and manage, and may have some stability issues. One specific technical limitation worth knowing before switching is that NocoDB's API is still in development, and may not have all the features and functionality that Airtable's API has. However, for teams who value data ownership and customization, and have the technical expertise to set up and manage a self-hosted solution, NocoDB is a good choice, and we recommend switching from Airtable to NocoDB.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams who value data ownership and customization, and have the technical expertise to set up and manage a self-hosted solution.
* Large teams or enterprises who need a highly scalable and flexible database solution, and have the resources to invest in setup and management.
* Teams who do not need a comprehensive set of built-in features, and are willing to develop their own custom solutions.
* Teams who are currently using Airtable's free plan, and are looking for a more cost-effective solution.
* Teams who value open-source software, and are willing to contribute to the development of NocoDB.

## FAQ
### Is NocoDB free?
Yes, NocoDB is free and open-source, and can be self-hosted on your own server or cloud platform.
### Can I use NocoDB with a small team?
Yes, NocoDB can be used with a small team, but it may require more technical expertise to set up and manage.
